web_title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup
book_title: Chapter 8: Reading the Tape — Trend, Volume & Momentum Opportunity
question: What Stan Weinstein stage is Cirrus Logic in across weekly, daily, and 4-hour timeframes, and is there any actionable short-term trading or options edge right now?

epigraph.quote: Never buy a stock in Stage 4 or beneath a declining 30-week moving average; wait for institutional accumulation to prove itself on the chart first.
epigraph.author: Stan Weinstein, Secrets for Profiting in Bull and Bear Markets

web_blocks.html: As of the November 24, 2026 close, Cirrus Logic trades at $115.72 (-1.26% on the session), sitting 35.86% below its 52-week high of $180.42 and 10.10% above its 52-week low of $105.10 [28]. A multi-timeframe inspection reveals a stock attempting an early, fragile stabilization after a severe 6-month drawdown (-33.36% over 6 months) [28], yet still trapped deeply beneath every major long-term institutional trend floor. Specifically, CRUS sits 12.53% below its declining 30-week simple moving average ($132.30) and 15.91% below its 200-day simple moving average ($137.61) [28]. On the shorter timeframe, shares are hovering directly on top of the flat 50-day SMA ($115.21, +0.44% extension), 20-day SMA ($115.50), and 10-week EMA ($115.19, +0.46% extension) [28].

Two deterministic classifiers capture this exact structural tension. Our `stage2_evaluation` engine classifies CRUS as **STAGE_1** (`WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT_RETEST`, `CAP_WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT`) because price has stopped making lower lows since the $105.10 shelf and is coiling tightly along its 50-day SMA ($115.21) and 10-week EMA ($115.19) with a neutral daily RSI of 50.62 and tight 12.41% Bollinger Band width [28]. Meanwhile, our `options_snapshot` multi-timeframe classifier flags CRUS as **STAGE4_BELOW_STRUCTURAL_FLOOR** because it remains decisively below both the 30-week SMA ($132.30) and 200-day SMA ($137.61) with a bearish weekly RSI of 44.16 and no confirmed 4-hour reversal turn (`ema20_4h` at $116.10 caps price above $115.72) [28]. Reconciling both lenses is straightforward: CRUS is in a **nascent Stage 1 basing attempt inside a damaged primary downtrend**—decisively **not** a confirmed Stage 2 uptrend.

web_blocks.title: 8.2 Institutional Flow, Short Interest & Sector Breadth Headwinds

web_blocks.html: Volume and ownership flows confirm the absence of institutional accumulation. Daily volume on November 24 was 766,100 shares—virtually flat at 0.99x the 30-day average of 775,973 shares (0.93x Finviz average volume) [27][28]. Institutional ownership remains high at 105.43% (reflecting short-share rehypothecation), but trailing institutional transactions declined -1.40% and insider transactions fell -9.87% (insider ownership is a modest 0.64%) [27]. Meanwhile, short interest stands at 3.57 million shares, or 7.21% of float (4.33 days to cover)—a meaningful bearish positioning footprint for a debt-free mid-cap semiconductor name [27].

Even more decisive is the top-down tape. Our November 24, 2026 market ledger confirms the S&P 500 is in a **Downtrend** with 10 distribution days over the last 25 sessions and only 27.8% of the market breadth pool trading above its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [41]. Within Electronic Technology, the **Semiconductors** industry is experiencing severe breadth liquidation: just 8.2% of semiconductor stocks sit above their 200-day EMA, only 2.0% sit above their 50-day EMA, and only 18.4% are outperforming the S&P 500 (sector rank 100) [28]. While CRUS showed relative resilience on November 24 (-1.26% vs. -11.25% for TXN and -17.37% for ADI) [28], buying a single-customer chipmaker below its 30-week SMA in a 10-distribution-day Downtrend violates core Weinstein trend discipline.

Is there an asymmetric short-term swing trade or call-convexity setup in CRUS right now? The data gives an unambiguous **no** on both counts. On the equity chart, the automated support zone ($113.46–$117.25) carries an algorithmically tight invalidation stop at $113.06—just $2.66 (0.62x ATR) below CMP, which invites routine noise stop-outs given CRUS's $4.29 daily ATR [28]. Moving the stop to a genuine structural shelf below the $105.10 52-week low ($104.50, or 2.62x ATR) exposes $11.22–$12.75 of downside risk against only $4.46 of upside to Pivot R1 ($120.18) or $8.75–$10.28 to Base fair value ($126.00)—a sub-1:1 reward-to-risk trap. On the options desk, `options_snapshot.py` stamps CRUS **`NOT_OPTIONABLE_OR_ILLIQUID`**: CRUS options bid-ask spreads exceed 14% or lack institutional open interest, making call spreads and LEAPS unviable due to immediate slippage drag. Traders and investors alike have zero edge forcing a position here.

book_paragraphs: Step back from the spreadsheets and look at Cirrus Logic's price chart with me. Charts are not fortune-telling devices; they are footprints of institutional supply and demand. And right now, the footprints on CRUS tell a story of heavy damage followed by an uneasy truce. At $115.72, the stock sits 35.86% below its 52-week high of $180.42. Over the past six months, CRUS has surrendered a third of its market value. Even though shares held up remarkably well on November 24—slipping just 1.26% on a brutal day when Texas Instruments plunged 11.25% and Analog Devices collapsed 17.37%—resilience on one ugly Tuesday does not equal an uptrend.

Apply Stan Weinstein's primary rule and the picture clarifies instantly. A confirmed Stage 2 uptrend requires price to trade above a rising 30-week simple moving average and above the 200-day moving average, backed by expanding volume and healthy sector breadth. Cirrus Logic fails every single one of those tests today. At $115.72, CRUS trades 12.53% below its 30-week SMA ($132.30) and 15.91% below its 200-day SMA ($137.61). Its weekly RSI sits at a soft 44.16. Every investor who bought shares between $120 and $180 over the past nine months is currently underwater, creating layers of overhead supply waiting to sell into rallies.

To be completely fair to the tape, CRUS is no longer in freefall. Since printing its 52-week low at $105.10, shares have carved out a tight horizontal coil right on top of the 50-day SMA ($115.21) and 10-week EMA ($115.19), compressing Bollinger Band width to 12.41% with a neutral daily RSI of 50.62. That is why our Stage 2 scanner classifies CRUS as an early Stage 1 basing candidate, while our multi-timeframe options lens classifies it as Stage 4 below its structural floor. Both perspectives point to the exact same practical conclusion: you are looking at a stock trying to build a floor, not a stock breaking out into institutional leadership.

Now zoom out to the macro and industry backdrop, because individual stocks rarely swim upstream against a tidal wave. As of November 24, 2026, the S&P 500 is locked in a 10-distribution-day Downtrend with just 27.8% of stocks above their 50-day moving average. Inside the Semiconductors industry, conditions are even bleaker: only 8.2% of chip stocks sit above their 200-day EMA and a stunning 2.0% sit above their 50-day EMA. Meanwhile, CRUS carries 7.21% of its float sold short (3.57 million shares, 4.33 days to cover) with zero volume accumulation surge (0.99x 30-day average volume).

What about using options to rent upside convexity cheaply while risking a small fixed dollar amount? We checked the listed U.S. options chain, and the market slammed that door shut as well. Cirrus Logic's options carry wide bid-ask spreads exceeding 14% with thin open interest, earning a strict NOT_OPTIONABLE_OR_ILLIQUID stamp. Paying 14%+ slippage on entry and exit destroys options expectancy before the stock even moves. Whether you are a short-term momentum trader or a position investor, the tape is telling you to keep your hands in your pockets until CRUS reclaims its 30-week moving average on genuine volume and semiconductor breadth heals.

Notice also what the anatomy of support and resistance tells us about trade construction. On a purely mechanical scan, the algorithm spots the 50-day SMA at $115.21 and draws a tight support buy zone between $113.46 and $117.25 with an invalidation stop at $113.06. Put yourself in the seat of a live portfolio manager for thirty seconds: Cirrus Logic's 14-day Average True Range is $4.29 per day. Putting a hard stop just $2.66 below the close—barely 0.62 times a single day's normal range—guarantees that an ordinary afternoon swing in the Nasdaq whipsaws you out at a loss. The only technically honest structural stop sits below the 52-week low of $105.10, around $104.50 (2.62x ATR), where buyers actually defended the stock during the autumn sell-off. Yet the moment you place your stop at $104.50, you are risking $11.22 per share from today's close to chase $10.28 of upside to our $126.00 Base fair value—and you still have to fight through heavy overhead supply at Pivot R1 ($120.18), Pivot R2 ($130.54), the 30-week SMA ($132.30), and the 200-day SMA ($137.61). Good traders refuse trades where the chart forces them to choose between a noise stop-out and a sub-1:1 payoff.

book_callouts.title: Narrator's Reflection: Why 'Less Bad' Is Not a Buy Signal
book_callouts.text: It is tempting to admire CRUS for dropping only 1.26% while analog titans TXN and ADI fell double digits on November 24. That relative stability reflects CRUS's $1.08 billion cash cushion and lower 14.6x P/E multiple. Yet relative stability below a falling 30-week moving average ($132.30) inside a 10-distribution-day market Downtrend is still dead money—and dead money carries real opportunity cost when cash earns nearly 5%.
